Treatment and Disinfection Processes: Escherichia coli (E. coli) or thermotolerant coliforms are not suitable indicators for the presence of Staphylococcus aureus in drinking water supplies, as faecal material is not the usual source of contamination for this organism. 2. Tsukamurella General Description: The genus Tsukamurella belongs to the family Nocardiaceae. These bacteria are Gram-positive, weakly or variably acid-fast, non-motile, obligate aerobic, and irregularly rod-shaped. They are actinomycetes related to Rhodococcus, Nocardia, and Mycobacterium. The genus was established in 1988 to classify organisms with unique chemical characteristics, including very long-chain (68–76 carbons), highly unsaturated mycolic acids, meso-diaminopimelic acid, and arabinogalactan, which are also found in the genus Corynebacterium. The type species is Tsukamurella paurometabola, and additional species such as T. wratislaviensis, T. inchonensis, T. pulmonis, T. tyrosinosolvens, and T. strandjordae were proposed in the 1990s. 3. Human Health Effects of Tsukamurella: Tsukamurella species primarily cause disease in immunocompromised individuals. Infections have been associated with chronic lung diseases, immune suppression (e.g., leukemia, tumors, HIV/AIDS), and post-operative wound infections. They have been reported in cases of catheter-related bacteremia, chronic lung infections, necrotizing tenosynovitis with subcutaneous abscesses, cutaneous and bone infections, meningitis, and peritonitis. 4. Source and Occurrence of Tsukamurella: These bacteria are environmental saprophytes found in soil, water, and foam (thick stable scum) in aeration vessels and sedimentation tanks of activated sludge systems. They are also present in heterotrophic plate count (HPC) populations in drinking water. 5. Routes of Exposure for Tsukamurella: Transmission appears to occur through devices such as catheters or lesions. The original source of contamination is often unknown. 6. Significance in Drinking Water: Tsukamurella organisms have been detected in drinking water supplies, but their significance remains unclear. There is no evidence linking these organisms in water to illness. As Tsukamurella is an environmental organism, E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms are not suitable indicators for its presence. 7. Vibrio General Description: Vibrio species are small, curved (comma-shaped), Gram-negative bacteria with a single polar flagellum. Pathogenic species include V. cholerae, V. parahaemolyticus, and V. vulnificus. V. cholerae is the only pathogenic species of significance in freshwater environments. Among its serotypes, only O1 and O139 cause classical cholera symptoms, characterized by severe watery diarrhea. The O1 serovar is further divided into classical and El Tor biotypes, with the latter responsible for the seventh cholera pandemic that began in 1961. 8. Human Health Effects of Vibrio cholerae: Cholera outbreaks continue to occur in developing regions. Symptoms are caused by a heat-labile cholera enterotoxin produced by toxigenic strains of V. cholerae O1/O139. While many infected individuals remain asymptomatic, symptomatic cases can range from mild to severe disease. Severe cases involve rice-water stools, leading to significant fluid and electrolyte loss, potentially up to 10–15 liters per day. Without treatment, severe dehydration and electrolyte imbalance can result in death, with fatality rates as high as 60% in untreated cases. However, effective diarrheal disease control programs can reduce fatalities to less than 1%. 9. Source and Occurrence of Vibrio cholerae: Non-toxigenic V. cholerae is widely distributed in water environments, while toxigenic strains are less common. Humans are a known source of toxigenic V. cholerae, which can be detected in sewage during outbreaks. Toxigenic strains have also been found associated with aquatic organisms such as copepods, mollusks, crustaceans, plants, algae, and cyanobacteria. The prevalence of V. cholerae decreases as water temperatures fall below 20°C. 10. Routes of Exposure for Vibrio cholerae: Cholera is typically transmitted via the fecal-oral route, primarily through the ingestion of fecally contaminated water and food. The high infectious dose required makes person-to-person transmission unlikely. 11. Significance in Drinking Water: Contamination of water due to poor sanitation is a major factor in cholera transmission. The presence of pathogenic V. cholerae O1 and O139 serotypes in drinking water supplies poses significant public health risks. V. cholerae is highly sensitive to disinfection processes. Control measures within a water safety plan include protecting raw water supplies from human waste, adequate treatment, and safeguarding water during distribution. 12. Yersinia General Description: The genus Yersinia belongs to the family Enterobacteriaceae and includes seven species, of which Y. pestis, Y. pseudotuberculosis, and certain serotypes of Y. enterocolitica are pathogenic to humans. Y. pestis causes bubonic plague, typically transmitted through contact with rodents and their fleas. Yersinia species are Gram-negative rods that are motile at 25°C but not at 37°C. 13. Human Health Effects of Yersinia: Y. enterocolitica penetrates intestinal mucosal cells, causing ulcerations in the terminal ileum. Yersiniosis generally presents as acute gastroenteritis with diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain. Other manifestations include enlarged, painful lymph nodes (buboes). The disease is more acute in children than adults. 14. Source and Occurrence of Yersinia: Domestic and wild animals are the primary reservoirs for Yersinia species. Pigs are the major reservoir for pathogenic Y. enterocolitica, while rodents and small animals are reservoirs for Y. pseudotuberculosis. Pathogenic Y. enterocolitica has been detected in sewage and polluted surface waters. Strains found in drinking water are more commonly non-pathogenic and of environmental origin. Some Yersinia species can replicate in water environments with trace organic nitrogen, even at temperatures as low as 4°C. 15. Routes of Exposure for Yersinia: Transmission occurs via the fecal-oral route, with food (e.g., meat, milk, and dairy products) being the primary source of infection. Contaminated water is also a potential source. Direct transmission from person to person or animals to humans is known to occur. 16. Significance in Drinking Water: Most Yersinia species detected in water are likely non-pathogenic. However, circumstantial evidence supports the transmission of Y. enterocolitica and Y. pseudotuberculosis to humans from untreated drinking water. The most likely source of pathogenic Yersinia species is human or animal waste. These organisms are sensitive to disinfection processes. Control measures include protecting raw water supplies from waste, adequate disinfection, and safeguarding water during distribution. Due to the potential for long survival and growth of some Yersinia strains in water, E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms are not reliable indicators for their presence. 17. Viral Pathogens: Waterborne viruses primarily infect the gastrointestinal tract and are excreted in the feces of infected individuals. Enteric viruses typically cause acute diseases with short incubation periods. Water may also play a role in transmitting other viruses with different modes of action. Some respiratory viruses, for example, may be excreted in feces, leading to potential water contamination and transmission through aerosols. Viruses excreted in urine, such as polyomaviruses, could also contaminate water and potentially cause long-term health effects, such as cancer. 18. Adenoviruses General Description: Adenoviruses belong to the family Adenoviridae and are classified into two genera: Mastadenovirus (mammalian hosts) and Aviadenovirus (avian hosts). They are widespread in nature, infecting birds, mammals, and amphibians. Human adenoviruses are classified into six groups (A–F) based on their physical, chemical, and biological properties. They consist of a double-stranded DNA genome within a non-enveloped icosahedral capsid, approximately 80 nm in diameter. Identification of serotypes 40 and 41 in environmental samples is typically based on polymerase chain reaction (PCR) techniques.
